passage: The colony park was still wet from the monsoon rain. Hansa slipped on the muddy slide steps and sat down hard, crying loudly, her frock streaked brown. Sahil stopped digging. He looked at the half glucose biscuit in his fist, then snapped it into two uneven pieces and held out the bigger one. 'Here. You have it.' He patted her knee three times, the way his Nani pats his back at bedtime. Hansa sniffed, took the biscuit and leaned against his shoulder.

qa.a: He snapped it into two uneven pieces and held out the bigger one to Hansa.

passage:
'Usha, why are you crying?'
'My balloon flew away.'
Nazia looked up at the red balloon drifting over the Eid lights strung across the building gate. Then she opened her fist. 'I have a nankhatai from Ammi. Look, I'll break it.'
'It's broken now.'
'It's for sharing. Half for you, half for me.'
'Your half is smaller.'
'That's okay.' Nazia patted Usha's arm. 'Don't cry. My balloon flew away last Eid also. We can wave to it.'
'Bye, balloon!'
'Bye!'
Usha chewed, still hiccupping, and waved with crumbs on both hands.

qa.a: Nazia had a nankhatai from Ammi.

qa.a: Nazia felt sorry for Usha and cared more about Usha feeling better than about the biscuit.

passage:
Winter note, Sunflower Room, Tuesday.
During outdoor time a cold wind blew Nilesh's woollen cap into the drain. He began sobbing and would not come back to the mat. Gautam watched for a moment, then walked over with his snack box. He broke his jam biscuit, gave one half to Nilesh and patted his back. 'Your cap is only wet. You can hold mine, it's warm.' Nilesh calmed within a minute. I dried the cap on the heater and told Gautam I had noticed him helping. He grinned. Next: a kindness story at circle time.

qa.q: Where did Nilesh's woollen cap end up?
qa.a: A cold wind blew it into the drain.

qa.q: What does Gautam's offer of his own cap suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt sympathy for Nilesh and wanted the sobbing to stop; he cared enough to give up half his biscuit and his warm cap.

qa.a: Telling Gautam the helping was noticed names his kindness for him, which makes it more likely he will do it again.

qa.q: How might Nilesh see Gautam after this?
qa.a: Nilesh may see Gautam as someone safe to go to when upset, since Gautam came over while he was sobbing.

passage: Hrithik, you ask why I still visit Savitri every Makar Sankranti. Sit, I'll tell you. I was ten, and that January kites filled the sky, but Savitri came back to school thin as a stick after a long fever. Her satchel was heavy with slates and books, so every day I carried it, mine on my back and hers in my arms, all the way to her lane. One evening she whispered that her father had lost his job at the mill and there was no money for kite string that year. 'Don't tell anyone, Nikita.' I didn't. Not the other girls, not even my own mother. On festival morning I just gave her half my string and said I had too much. Fifty years later she still laughs about my 'too much'.

qa.q: What did Nikita carry every day while Savitri was weak?
qa.a: Savitri's heavy satchel, carried all the way to Savitri's lane.

qa.q: Why did Nikita keep Savitri's news from everyone, even at home?
qa.a: Nikita felt loyal and protective towards Savitri, who had trusted Nikita with something painful, and that trust mattered more than talking.

qa.q: Nikita gave Savitri half the kite string and claimed to have too much. Why was that a good choice?
qa.a: It let Savitri join the festival without being pitied, and it kept the secret safe because nobody needed to know why.

qa.q: How might Savitri have felt about Nikita's 'too much' story?
qa.a: Savitri probably felt grateful and relieved not to be pitied; that is why she still laughs about it fifty years later.

grounding: An elder recalls a childhood of carrying Savitri's bag during illness and keeping her private worry, loyalty to someone close.

passage: The monsoon had turned the school path into a brown stream, and the bus was not running. Indu was still weak after a week of fever, so Anand slung her bag over his own and held the umbrella over both of them. His shoes filled with water. Twice he slipped; twice he kept the bags dry against his chest. At the corner shop Indu stopped to catch her breath. 'Don't tell the others I cried in the sick room today,' she said. 'I've missed so much work.' 'I won't,' Anand said. Next morning, when a classmate asked why Indu's eyes had been red, Anand shrugged. 'Rain gets in your eyes,' he said, and changed the subject to cricket.

qa.q: What did Anand hold over both of them?
qa.a: He held the umbrella over both of them.

qa.a: He felt protective of Indu and determined to keep his promise, so he brushed the question off lightly.

qa.a: She can lean on him while she is weak and trust him with something embarrassing, which likely makes her feel safer and less alone.

passage: Two days before the Durga Puja holidays, the Kolkata lane outside school smelt of fresh paint from the pandal going up. Saurabh coughed all through the last period, his nose red. When the bell rang, Dilnaz picked up his bag before he could. 'I can carry it,' he croaked. 'You carry your cough,' she said. Walking past the half-built pandal, he told her very quietly that the poem about the goddess's eyes in the school puja magazine was his, printed under a made-up name. 'Nobody knows. They'd tease me.' At the gate their friends were guessing who had written it. Dilnaz only smiled, and handed Saurabh his bag at his door.

qa.a: That the poem about the goddess's eyes in the school puja magazine was his, printed under a made-up name.

passage: So you want to know when Pune started feeling like home? Honestly, it was a Tuesday in my second month here. My name's Kunal, by the way, and back then I was a mess. I'd called home, heard the pressure cooker whistle in our kitchen in Nagpur, and after hanging up I just sat on my bed staring at the wall. My flatmate Hemant knocked, didn't ask anything, and put a steel glass of ginger chai on my desk. Then he sat on the floor and complained about his lab partner, loudly, for about an hour. I laughed twice. He did the same thing the next Tuesday, and the one after. I never asked him to. I think that's the point: he just kept turning up, so I stopped feeling like a guest in my own life.

qa.q: What did Hemant put on Kunal's desk?
qa.a: A steel glass of ginger chai.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling after hanging up the call home?
qa.a: Kunal felt homesick and low, sitting on the bed staring at the wall after hearing the pressure cooker whistle back home.

qa.q: What makes Hemant's way of helping work so well?
qa.a: It asks nothing of Kunal: Hemant brings chai, fills the silence and comes back each week, so the care feels steady rather than a one-time rescue.

qa.q: How might Hemant see those Tuesday evenings?
qa.a: Hemant may see them as ordinary time with a flatmate rather than a big favour, which is partly why Kunal found them easy to accept.

grounding: A homesick student describes a flatmate's unasked, repeated chai visits making the city feel like home.

passage:
Monday, week one: Vikas ate dinner alone in his room in the Chennai flat, a packet of biscuits and a photo of the tea garden behind his house in Assam. The ceiling fan was loud. He did not go out when he heard Abhinav's music in the hall.
Thursday: a knock. Abhinav stood there with two cups of lemon tea. 'I made too much. Also, I'm bad at being alone.' He stayed till midnight, asking about the hills, the rain, Vikas's grandmother's pickles.
Two Sundays later: nobody had asked, but the tea kept arriving, Thursdays and sometimes Mondays. When his mother called, Vikas said, 'Wait, Ma, my flatmate is shouting about rice,' and heard himself laughing. He did not reach for the photo that night.

qa.q: What did Abhinav bring on Thursday?
qa.a: Abhinav brought two cups of lemon tea.

qa.q: What had changed in how Vikas felt by the third beat?
qa.a: Vikas felt settled and more at home; laughing on the call and not reaching for the photo show the homesick loneliness had eased.

qa.q: What small step could Vikas take now to keep this bond steady?
qa.a: He could return the kindness his own way, perhaps sharing the grandmother's pickles with Abhinav, so the care flows both ways.

qa.q: What might Abhinav gain from these evenings?
qa.a: Abhinav admitted being bad at being alone, so the tea visits probably ease his own loneliness too, not only Vikas's.

grounding: Over two weeks a lonely student is brought tea and company unasked and begins to feel he belongs.

passage: You're packing for Bengaluru, Sahil, so let me tell you something your Usha Maasi never told anyone. My first year in Delhi, I cried into my pillow every night so the other girls in the hostel wouldn't hear. The food tasted of nothing. Then Onam came, and I couldn't go home; the train ticket was more than I had. That evening Parveen, my roommate, the loud one from Lucknow, came in with two cups of tea and a banana leaf she had begged from the mess. 'I don't know how to make your sadya,' she said, 'but I brought rice and I brought me.' We sat on the floor and ate with our hands. She never made a speech about it. She just came back every night that week with tea. That's when the room became my room, beta.

qa.q: What did Parveen bring on Onam evening?
qa.a: Two cups of tea and a banana leaf she had begged from the mess.

qa.q: How did Usha feel before that Onam evening, and what shows it?
qa.a: She felt deeply homesick and lonely; she cried into her pillow every night and said the food tasted of nothing.

qa.q: Parveen brought rice and herself instead of trying to cook a proper sadya. Why did that choice work?
qa.a: It showed she cared without pretending to fix everything; her plain, repeated company told Usha she belonged, which a perfect meal alone could not.

qa.q: How might Parveen have seen that evening?
qa.a: Parveen probably saw it as a small, natural thing to do for a roommate far from home, which is why she never made a speech about it.

grounding: An aunt recalls a hostel roommate who brought tea and company unasked, making her feel safe far from home.

passage:
Dear Nirmala Didi,
Thank you for thinking of me for Chinnu's wedding shopping. You know I love that girl, and I've loved doing the lists and tailor runs for every cousin so far. This time I have to say no to the full job. The last three weekends I've driven Amma to her physio, covered double shifts at the hospital and helped Raju move flats. On Sunday I fell asleep standing at the stove. I don't want to show up for Chinnu grumpy and half-present.
What I can do: the jewellery trip on the 14th, and I'll send you my tailor's number tonight. The rest I'm handing back, with love. I'd rather be useful for years than burnt out by March.
Your Minakshi

qa.a: The jewellery trip on the 14th, plus sending the tailor's number tonight.

qa.q: What is Minakshi feeling while writing this refusal?
qa.a: Minakshi feels exhausted and a little torn: there is real love for Chinnu, but also worry about turning up grumpy and half-present.

qa.q: Why is offering one specific task better than a flat no here?
qa.a: It keeps the relationship warm and shows real care while protecting Minakshi's energy; a clear limit is easier for Nirmala to plan around than a vague maybe.

qa.q: How might Nirmala take this letter?
qa.a: Nirmala may be disappointed at first, but the honest reasons and the concrete offer make the no easier to respect than to resent.

grounding: A generous young adult writes to decline a big family task when exhausted while offering a smaller part.

passage: You asked what I've learned this year. Okay, here's one. I'm Akash, and for about three years I was everyone's free tech support. Chacha's printer, my cousin's laptop, my friend Nandini's router: every Sunday, gone. I liked being needed, I really did. Then in March, after a month of late nights at work, Nandini called: could I help her shift flats that Sunday? My stomach dropped. I heard myself say, 'I can't this weekend, I'm running on empty. I'll bring dinner to your new place on Saturday and set up the wifi then.' There was a pause, and then she said, 'Oh, thank God, I thought you'd never say no to anything.' We laughed. I slept eleven hours that Sunday. And the Saturday dinner was actually fun, because I wasn't resentful.

qa.q: What did Akash offer Nandini instead of helping on Sunday?
qa.a: To bring dinner to the new place on Saturday and set up the wifi then.

qa.q: What did Akash's stomach dropping suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Akash felt dread and exhaustion at one more request, torn between liking being needed and having nothing left to give.

qa.q: What could Akash do next time a relative asks for weekend tech help?
qa.a: Akash could check energy first and offer a specific time that fits, instead of saying yes automatically out of habit.

qa.q: How does Nandini see Akash's no?
qa.a: She sees it as a relief and a healthy sign, since she had worried Akash never said no to anything 🙂

grounding: A young adult who always helps says no when running on empty, offers a smaller favour, and stays generous.

passage: I share a desk row with Payal at the insurance office, so I see a lot. She is the one who covers your shift when your kid is sick, who remembers birthdays, who drove the new trainee to the station in the rain. Last Friday our manager asked her to stay late again to finish someone else's claims. I watched her rub her eyes, then smile and say, 'Not tonight. I've stayed late four days this week and I'm starting to make mistakes. I can take two of them first thing Monday.' The manager blinked, then nodded. On Monday she came in early, finished both, and brought samosas for the team. I don't know what went on in her head. But I'm Vaibhav, the one who never says no, and I left at six that Friday too.

qa.q: How many days had Payal already stayed late that week?
qa.a: She had stayed late four days that week.

qa.q: What might Payal have been feeling when she rubbed her eyes before answering?
qa.a: She was probably tired and a little worried about making mistakes, yet calm enough to say no kindly and offer a Monday plan.

qa.q: Which part of Payal's reply made the no easier for the manager to accept?
qa.a: She gave a clear reason, four late days and mistakes creeping in, and offered a specific time, first thing Monday, for two of the claims.

qa.q: How does watching Payal affect Vaibhav?
qa.a: Vaibhav, who never says no, sees that a limit can be set politely and still be accepted, and leaves at six that Friday too.

passage: Holi was two days away and the colony compound in Pune was full of kids testing water pistols. When the older ones picked teams for a chasing game, Pradeep stood at the edge, hands in pockets. His family had moved from a village in Bihar in the summer, and Deepika barely knew him. 'Not him,' said the captain. 'He doesn't even know our rules.' Deepika, already picked, stepped out of the line. 'That's unfair. Nobody knew the rules the first time. He should play.' A few kids groaned. 'Then you teach him,' the captain said. 'Fine.' Deepika walked Pradeep through it: tag, freeze, unfreeze. By the third round he was the fastest runner on her team, and the captain went quiet.

qa.q: Where had Pradeep's family moved from?
qa.a: From a village in Bihar, in the summer.

qa.q: Why did Deepika step out of the line?
qa.a: She felt indignant that Pradeep was being shut out just for being new, even though she barely knew him, and wanted the game to be fair.

qa.q: How could an adult in the colony back up what Deepika did?
qa.a: They could thank her for speaking up and make it a habit that every child can join team picks, so newcomers don't depend on one brave kid.

qa.q: What is it like for Pradeep when Deepika speaks up?
qa.a: Pradeep goes from standing alone at the edge to being taught and welcomed, which likely feels like relief; he ends up the fastest runner on her team.

grounding: A girl objects when a newcomer from another region is kept out of a game, fairness beyond her own friends.

'Why isn't Tsering playing?' Harish asked, tapping the bat on the steps.
'It's our building's team,' said Minakshi. 'He's from the settlement.'
'He was standing there the whole time. He even has a glove.'

Minakshi snorted. 'Fine. But you're explaining the sixes rule.'

passage: Last Ramzan, after iftar, we played football in the lane every night under the tube light. I'm Irfan, and I was usually goalkeeper. One night Francis from the church end of the street came with his own ball and asked to join. Someone said, 'This is our game, go play with your people.' Everyone laughed. I didn't. My stomach felt hot. I said, 'He brought a ball. And it's everybody's lane. Anyone can play.' It came out louder than I meant. For a second I thought they'd kick me out too. Then Sameer shrugged and said Francis could be on my side. Francis scored twice. When I think about it now, I'm glad I said it, even though my voice shook.

qa.q: What did Francis bring when he asked to join?
qa.a: His own ball.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel just before speaking up?
qa.a: Irfan felt a hot anger at the laughing, and fear of being kicked out too; the shaking voice shows how nervous it was.

qa.q: What could the lane's players agree so this doesn't depend on one person speaking up?
qa.a: They could agree that anyone from the lane who turns up gets a turn, so nobody has to argue it each night.

qa.q: What would it be like for Francis if nobody had spoken up?
qa.a: Francis would have walked away laughed at and shut out of his own street, likely feeling hurt and unwelcome.

passage:
'Hold the sapling straight, Mohit, I'm filling the soil.'
'Why are you so serious today? It's just a neem.'
Kamal pressed the earth down with both palms. 'Did you see the floods on the news? A whole village school was under water. Kids our age were on rooftops.'
'That's far from here, yaar.'
'That's the thing. Sir said last week the rivers and forests are all connected: cut trees in one place, soil washes away, floods get worse somewhere else. So maybe it's not that far.'
'You think one neem is going to stop a flood?'
'No.' Kamal wiped his forehead, leaving a streak of mud. 'But I keep thinking about those kids. I can't do nothing. This is something.'
Mohit was quiet, then picked up the second sapling. 'Okay. Show me how deep.'

qa.q: What kind of tree were they planting first?
qa.a: A neem.

qa.q: What might Kamal be worried about?
qa.a: Kamal is worried and upset about the flood-hit kids on rooftops, and feels unable to do nothing even though they are far away.

qa.q: What could Kamal do beyond planting to act on this concern?
qa.a: He could join or start a school flood-relief collection with a teacher's help, so the worry also turns into help for the people he is thinking about.

qa.q: How does Mohit's view change during the conversation?
qa.a: Mohit starts by seeing the drive as a small chore and the floods as far away, but after hearing Kamal quietly picks up the second sapling and asks to learn.

passage: It was the pictures Urmila sent in August that got to me. We became pen friends through a school exchange, and her village near the Kosi floods almost every monsoon. That month her whole courtyard was brown water, and her little brother's school books were drying on the roof. I'm Simran, and I live in a dry flat in Jaipur; I had never thought about rain as something that takes things away. So when our eco-club announced a tree-planting drive along the city's dry riverbed, I signed up first. Our teacher explained how bare slopes let rain run off faster and how rivers carry that water far. I know my forty saplings won't save Urmila's courtyard. But planting them felt less like charity and more like admitting we are on the same map. I still text her before every monsoon.

qa.q: What was drying on the roof in Urmila's pictures?
qa.a: Her little brother's school books.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when the August pictures came?
qa.a: Simran felt shaken and worried for Urmila, and uneasy at never having thought of rain as something that takes things away.

qa.q: What else could Simran do that would help Urmila's family more directly?
qa.a: Simran could ask the eco-club teacher about a proper flood-relief collection, and keep listening to what Urmila says the family actually needs.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel getting Simran's texts before every monsoon?
qa.a: Urmila may feel remembered and less alone, knowing someone in a dry city thinks about the family's home when the rains come 🤍

passage:
Eco-club note, Saturday planting drive, Class 9 volunteers.
Ankita arrived early and planted more saplings than anyone, but she was quiet, not her usual self. Her friend Nandini suggested a stall at the school fair for flood relief. Ankita brightened and started listing what they could sell. passage:
Monday: Darshan, Jatin's cousin, called from the hostel office. 'You're on the allotment committee. Just put me on the ground-floor list. Nobody will notice.' Jatin said he'd think about it, then lay awake counting: forty-two first-years waiting, some from far-off districts with no relatives in the city.
Wednesday: he walked past the notice board, found Darshan's name at thirty-one on the queue list, and felt sick. Darshan's family had lent him their scooter all last year. Saying no felt like betrayal; saying yes felt like cheating strangers.
Friday: he met Darshan at the tea stall. 'I can't move you up. It wouldn't be fair to the others. But I'll help you find a paying-guest room nearby till your turn comes, and I'll move your stuff myself.' Darshan sulked, then asked which lanes were quietest.

qa.q: Where was Darshan's name on the queue list?
qa.a: At thirty-one on the queue list.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling on Wednesday?
qa.a: Jatin felt torn and sick: refusing seemed like betraying family who had helped him, while agreeing seemed like cheating strangers.

qa.q: Why is Jatin's Friday answer better than a plain yes or no?
qa.a: It keeps the list fair for the other first-years but still shows loyalty, because Jatin offers real help with a room and the move.

qa.q: How might the first-years from far-off districts be affected if Jatin had said yes?
qa.a: One of them could have lost a ground-floor place to someone with connections, and learned that the list does not really count.

grounding: Across a week a young man weighs fairness to strangers against loyalty to his cousin and finds a considered answer.

passage: Kamal, you asked how I decide when a friend asks for a favour at work. Let me tell you about my final year of college. I was twenty-one, helping the office sort scholarship forms. My closest friend, Leela, had missed one signed document. Twelve other forms had already gone into the rejected pile for exactly that. That night Leela cried on my shoulder: her father's shop had failed, and without the scholarship she'd have to drop out. 'Uma, just slip it in,' she begged. Nobody checked my work. I didn't sleep. By morning I knew I couldn't bend the rule for her alone. So I went to the office head and asked whether all thirteen could get a week to submit the missing paper. Nine of them made it, Leela too. She didn't talk to me for two days, though, and that hurt.

qa.q: How many forms had already gone into the rejected pile?
qa.a: Twelve other forms.

qa.q: What did Uma's sleepless night show about how Uma felt?
qa.a: It shows Uma felt torn and troubled between loyalty to a desperate Leela and fairness to the twelve others rejected for the same mistake.

qa.q: Uma asked the office head for a week for all thirteen students. Why was that a wise turning point?
qa.a: It kept things fair because the rule changed for everyone rather than for one friend, and still gave Leela a real chance; nine made it, Leela too.

qa.q: Why might Leela have stopped talking to Uma for two days?
qa.a: Leela was likely hurt and scared, wanting a friend to rescue her quietly, so being treated like everyone else felt like betrayal at first.

subtype: Universal principle against loyalty to own circle [Actor]
passage: They were already forty minutes late for Kiran's sister's engagement when the car scraped the side of a parked auto-rickshaw in a narrow Madurai lane. The driver wasn't around. 'Nobody saw,' Kiran said, hands tight on the wheel. 'Let's go. Please, Karthik, Amma will be furious if we're later.' Karthik looked at the dented door, at the driver's name painted on the back, at a child's school bag on the seat. That man would lose days of fares getting it fixed. But Kiran was his oldest friend, and Kiran's mother had fed him through every exam. His phone buzzed: 'Where are you both??' Karthik took a breath. 'Give me five minutes. We leave a number, or I wait here alone and you go.' Kiran stared, then sighed, pulled out a receipt and wrote a phone number to tuck under the wiper.

qa.q: What was on the auto-rickshaw's seat?
qa.a: A child's school bag.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling as he looked at the dented door?
qa.a: Karthik felt torn: sympathy for the driver who would lose fares, and loyalty and gratitude towards Kiran and Kiran's mother.

qa.q: What went right in how Karthik handled the pressure?
qa.a: He paused and offered a concrete plan instead of choosing in a panic, so the driver was treated fairly without abandoning Kiran.

qa.q: How might the auto driver feel on finding the note?
qa.a: The driver would likely feel relieved and respected, knowing someone took responsibility instead of vanishing.

grounding: Under time pressure a young man weighs fairness to a stranger against loyalty to his oldest friend and works it through.

subtype: Turning wide concern into local action [Response]
passage: People think caring about the world means big speeches. I'm Tenzin, twenty-five, and I used to be the loudest person in the group chat about climate and fairness. Then Raghav, who runs the ironing cart downstairs, asked me why I never came to the residents' meetings. I had no answer. So this year I tried small things. Saturday mornings I help at the community library, stamping books for kids from both sides of the road. Before the ward election I actually read what each candidate had done about our drains, instead of voting the way my friends did. And I learnt the names of the women who sweep our lane: Rani and Bano. Raghav says I've gone soft. Maybe. But the drain outside finally got fixed after we all wrote to the councillor together, and that felt better than a hundred posts.

qa.q: Where does Tenzin help on Saturday mornings?
qa.a: At the community library, stamping books for kids from both sides of the road.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel when Raghav asked about the residents' meetings?
qa.a: Tenzin felt caught out and a little embarrassed, having no answer despite being so loud about fairness in the group chat.

qa.q: What is one small local step someone like Tenzin could add next?
qa.a: Tenzin could start going to the residents' meetings Raghav mentioned, giving the concern for the lane a regular place to become action.

qa.a: Raghav teases that Tenzin has gone soft, but likely sees a neighbour who now shows up in person instead of only talking online.

subtype: Turning wide concern into local action [Response]
passage: I'm Nazia, and Nitin has lived across the landing from me for two years. Honestly, when he moved in I thought he was one of those people who post about saving the planet and never take out their own trash. I was wrong. Every Sunday evening I see him leave with a cloth bag of chalk and storybooks for the class he runs for the construction workers' kids behind our building. During the water cuts last May, he carried buckets up four floors for old Mrs D'Souza and for the Pandeys alike, and wrote the tanker timings in Hindi, Marathi and English on the notice board. On election day he knocked to ask if I'd found my polling booth, then argued with me for ten minutes about the drainage promises. I don't know what drives him. I only know the building is kinder since he came.

qa.q: In which languages did Nitin write the tanker timings?
qa.a: In Hindi, Marathi and English.

qa.q: What does Nitin's habit of carrying buckets for everyone suggest about his feelings?
qa.a: It suggests real care and respect for all his neighbours, not just people like him; he helped Mrs D'Souza and the Pandeys alike.

qa.q: What makes Nitin's approach more lasting than one big gesture?
qa.a: His acts are small and regular, Sunday classes, notices, checking on neighbours, so people can count on them and the habits spread.

qa.q: How has Nazia's view of Nitin changed?
qa.a: Nazia first suspected Nitin only posted about big ideals, but after watching his steady small acts now thinks the building is kinder since he came.

grounding: A neighbour watches a young man turn wide concern into steady local acts for people of every background.

subtype: Turning wide concern into local action [Response]
passage:
First week of June: Jatin spent a Sunday arguing online about inequality until two in the morning and woke up feeling hollow. His flatmate Sachin, stirring poha, said, 'You care about the whole country. Do you know the watchman's name?'
Two weeks later: Jatin sat at a folding table outside the ration shop with Sachin, helping neighbours fill in voter registration forms: a Bengali-speaking carpenter, a Tamil widow, two college students from Manipur. He learnt to say 'next, please' in three languages and found out the watchman was called Ramesh.
Late July: before the municipal vote, Jatin went to the candidates' meeting in the school hall and asked each one about the broken streetlights on the east lanes. Walking home, he greeted Ramesh by name. The online arguments had stopped. He felt, oddly, more useful than angry.

qa.q: Where did Jatin sit with Sachin two weeks later?
qa.a: At a folding table outside the ration shop.

qa.q: How did Jatin feel after the late-night online arguing?
qa.a: He woke up feeling hollow, as if all that concern had gone nowhere.

qa.q: What small step helped Jatin move from anger to action?
qa.a: Sachin's question about the watchman's name nudged him to start local: registration forms, a candidates' meeting, greeting neighbours by name.

qa.q: What would change for the neighbours if Jatin had kept only arguing online?
qa.a: The carpenter, the widow and the students might not have had help with their forms, and Ramesh would still be nameless to him.

grounding: Over two months a young man shifts from online outrage to local action: helping neighbours register, questioning candidates, knowing names.

subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
passage: Dear Diary, Dussehra fair day!!! Ganga here, too excited to sleep. I begged Lakshmi Akka to take me on the tallest slide, the yellow one that goes round and round, and she said, 'Only if the man checks your height.' I stood on my toes. I PASSED. My tummy flipped all the way down and I screamed and then I wanted to go AGAIN. Then I tried the bumper cars, the mirror house, and I asked for the ride that spins you upside down, which Akka said no to, so I did the camel ride instead. Boring. Standing in the food queue was the WORST, worse than being scared. I am going to be a pilot, or a stunt lady. Tomorrow is school. Ugh. Nothing new ever happens at school.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi Akka say about the tallest slide?
qa.a: Only if the man checks Ganga's height.

qa.q: What was Ganga feeling on the way down the slide?
qa.a: Ganga felt thrilled and a bit scared at once; the tummy flip and the scream turned straight into wanting to go again.

qa.q: How could Lakshmi Akka use Ganga's love of excitement safely?
qa.a: She could keep offering new, safe challenges, like rides with height checks or a new sport, while holding firm on unsafe ones, as she did with the upside-down ride.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi Akka feel after a day at the fair with Ganga?
qa.a: Lakshmi Akka is probably amused but also watchful and a bit tired from judging every new thrill Ganga begs for.

grounding: A girl's festival-day diary shows her craving the tallest slide and every new ride, finding boredom worse than fear.

subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
passage: The mustard fields around Rampura were yellow to the horizon, and Sarika had been bored for three whole days of winter holidays. She had counted the buffaloes, climbed the same neem, and swung on the same tyre till it felt like homework. So when Yusuf, the tailor's son from next door, came pedalling his tall black bicycle along the canal road, she ran after him. 'Teach me! Down the slope, the steep one!' 'You'll fly into the canal.' 'Anything is better than the tyre. Please!' Yusuf laughed. 'Flat road first. If you can stop without falling, then the slope, and I run beside you.' Sarika wobbled, crashed into a mustard row, laughed, and got straight back on. By sunset she was shrieking down the slope, Yusuf panting behind.

qa.q: What had Sarika swung on until it felt like homework?
qa.a: The same tyre.

qa.q: Why did Sarika beg to go down the steep slope?
qa.a: She was desperately bored and craved excitement; a little risk felt far better to her than another day on the tyre.

qa.q: What did Yusuf's plan get right?
qa.a: He didn't crush Sarika's thirst for thrills; he made it safer with the flat road first and running beside her on the slope.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel running behind Sarika at sunset?
qa.a: Yusuf is probably tired and a little nervous, but also amused and proud of how fast she learned.

grounding: In a winter village a girl who finds sameness unbearable begs to try a steep bicycle slope.

subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
passage: The winter festival in their Hokkaido town had ice slides taller than houses, and Hiroshi wanted every one. After the small slide twice and the snow maze once, he was hopping on the spot. 'The big one, Kaito! The one with the curve!' Kaito, his older brother, looked at the queue and the steep blue ice. 'Mum said the small ones.' 'The small ones are for babies. I'm going to die of boredom.' 'You'll bump your head, more like.' Hiroshi tugged his brother's glove. 'I'll wear the helmet they give out. And I'll sit, not lie down.' Kaito read the sign by the steps: helmets required, young children with an older companion. He sighed. 'Fine. I'm right behind you.' At the bottom Hiroshi's cheeks were pink, and he was already pointing at the snow rafting.

qa.q: What did the sign by the steps say?
qa.a: Helmets required, young children with an older companion.

qa.q: What does Hiroshi's hopping on the spot suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was restless and excited, eager for something bigger than the small slides he now found boring.

qa.q: What could Mum do at home to feed Hiroshi's craving for thrills safely?
qa.a: She could plan new, safe challenges, like a climbing class or a new sport, so Hiroshi gets excitement without chasing risky ones.

qa.q: What is it like for Kaito to be in charge of Hiroshi at the festival?
qa.a: Kaito is caught between Mum's rule and his brother's pleading; feeling responsible, he checks the sign and goes right behind him.

grounding: At a winter festival abroad a boy begs for the tallest ice slide and every new game, finding boredom worse than risk.

subtype: Conformity: follows rules to avoid upsetting others [Actor]
passage: In the monsoon term at the school in Sonpur, Dhruv's shirt was always tucked, his hair oiled flat, his slate wiped before the bell. He never used the old word his grandmother used for 'yes', because the other boys laughed at village talk, even though they all came from villages. When Sarita Madam asked who wanted the class outing to be to the new dam, where the water roared after the rains, Dhruv's hand twitched. He had dreamt of that dam for weeks. But Mohan and the others shouted 'Temple!' and looked around to see who disagreed. Dhruv raised his hand for the temple. At home he told his grandmother the outing would be fun. Then he went out and stood by the flooded paddy, throwing stones, very quiet.

qa.q: Which outing did Dhruv raise his hand for?
qa.a: The temple.

qa.q: What might Dhruv be feeling as he throws stones by the paddy?
qa.a: He is probably disappointed and sad, having buried his wish for the dam to avoid the other boys' disapproval.

qa.q: How could Sarita Madam make it safer for children like Dhruv to share their real choice?
qa.a: She could take the vote on folded paper slips instead of shouted answers, so no one has to look around to see who disagrees.

qa.q: How might Dhruv's grandmother see his quietness after school?
qa.a: She might sense something is wrong despite his cheerful words, and could gently ask what he really wanted.

grounding: A village boy keeps every rule and hides his real choice to avoid the group's disapproval.

subtopic: Schwartz values: stimulation, achievement, power, security, conformity, tradition
subtype: Conformity: follows rules to avoid upsetting others [Actor]
passage: In December the Toronto classroom smelled of wet mittens. Wei hung his coat on the third hook, exactly as the chart said, and sat with his hands folded before the bell, the way nobody else bothered to. He wore the same grey hoodie as half the class and spoke only in quiet, careful English, even at lunch. When Ms Carter asked for song ideas for the winter concert, Yosef's hand shot up. 'My grandpa's Hanukkah song! I can teach it.' The class clapped. Wei had a song too, the one his nai nai sang at New Year, with the drum part he loved. His hand lifted an inch and dropped. What if they thought it was strange? What if Ms Carter sighed? That afternoon he painted Yosef's candles on the backdrop, perfectly inside the lines.

qa.q: Where did Wei hang his coat?
qa.a: On the third hook, exactly as the chart said.

qa.q: Why did Wei's hand drop after lifting an inch?
qa.a: Wei was afraid the class would find the song strange and that Ms Carter might disapprove, so the fear buried the wish to share it.

qa.q: What could Ms Carter do to draw out quieter children like Wei?
qa.a: She could collect song ideas on slips or check in with Wei privately, so sharing doesn't mean risking disapproval in front of everyone.

qa.q: What would change if Wei had spoken up like Yosef?
qa.a: The concert might include the nai nai's New Year song with its drum part, and Wei might learn that ideas are welcomed, not judged.

grounding: A boy abroad follows every class rule and blends in, and swallows his own song idea for fear of disapproval.

passage: The week before Diwali, the school corridor was strung with paper lanterns, and Class 6B was planning its stall. Sudha sat in the front row with her dupatta pinned the regulation way and her notebook margins ruled in red, as the teacher liked. Varun, the class monitor, stood at the board. 'Crackers stall, final. Everyone agrees, right?' Sudha did not agree. Last year her dog had shivered under the bed for three nights. She had written 'diya-painting stall instead?' at the bottom of her page. Her pen hovered. Twenty-nine heads nodded. 'Right,' she said, the same as everyone, and crossed out her line so neatly nobody could read it. At the bell she got a star for tidy work, and walked home kicking a pebble all the way.

qa.q: What had Sudha written at the bottom of her page?
qa.a: 'Diya-painting stall instead?'

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling when she crossed out her line?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and afraid of standing out against twenty-nine nodding heads, so she hid her opinion; kicking the pebble shows her frustration.

qa.a: She could quietly show her idea to Varun or the teacher after class, a small first step before speaking to the whole room.

qa.a: Varun might be open to a diya stall; the monitor may simply not know anyone disagreed.
